1.5a — Movement II: Speed, deltaTime & Tuning

Movement works, but does it feel right? In game development, feel is the intersection of physics, math, and tuning. Today you compare the different functions Unity provides for moving objects, learn why Time.deltaTime is critical for fair gameplay, and tune your character's speed knobs live.

Read the Docs ~15 min

In Unity, there is rarely just one way to solve a problem. Depending on your game's design, different movement functions offer different advantages. Read this comparison of four common Unity movement techniques:

Movement TechniqueHow It WorksBest Used For
transform.Translate(vector) Directly offsets the object's coordinates. Bypasses the physics simulation during movement. Simple top-down games, moving UI, linear projectiles, bullets without gravity.
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) Sweeps the physics body to the target position, stopping cleanly against solid colliders. Kinematic characters, moving platforms, top-down games that must never clip into walls.
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity = vector Assigns a direct velocity vector to the physics body. Unity's physics engine handles movement. Snappy platformers, arcade physics, carrying momentum across surfaces.
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) Applies a physical push or impulse to the object, factoring in mass, drag, and inertia. Jumping, thrusters, ice physics, knockback from explosions or enemy hits.

Socratic: Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

  1. What happens if a high-speed character uses transform.Translate to move through a thin wall? (Hint: If the character jumps 2 units in one frame, what happens to the 0.5-unit wall in between?)
  2. In what scenarios would you choose Rigidbody2D.MovePosition over transform.Translate?
  3. Why would a game about a spaceship drifting in space prefer AddForce over Translate?
  4. For our top-down overworld, why is starting with transform.Translate clean and simple for learning?
Build Lab ~20 min

Code defaults vs. Inspector overrides. Look at the top of PlayerController.cs:

[SerializeField] private float xSpeed = 5.0f;
[SerializeField] private float ySpeed = 5.0f;

When you write = 5.0f in code, you are setting a fallback default. However, because these fields have [SerializeField], Unity stores the actual value inside the scene file (Overworld.unity). If you change the value in the Inspector, the Inspector override wins every time!

The live-tuning workflow:

  1. Press Play in Unity. Walk around the overworld.
  2. While the game is running, select the Player in the Hierarchy. In the Inspector, change xSpeed to 3. Walk around. Too sluggish?
  3. Change xSpeed to 12. Notice how responsive and rapid it feels.
  4. Test several numbers until you find the speed that feels right for exploration (try between 4 and 7).
  5. Remember your favorite number, exit Play mode, and set that value in edit mode so it saves permanently!
Remember the play-mode rule: Any value you change while the Play button is blue resets when you stop the game. Use play mode to find your number, then enter it in edit mode to keep it.

Bug Hunt: The deltaTime Abstraction

  1. Temporarily delete * Time.deltaTime from xVector in Update(). Run the game. What happens when you tap D?
  2. If a game runs at 60 frames per second on your laptop and 240 frames per second on a high-end desktop, how many times farther would the player move on the faster machine without Time.deltaTime?
  3. Why is Time.deltaTime considered an essential abstraction for multi-platform game development?
Tinker ~15 min

Tinker: Asymmetric Movement & Feel

  1. In the Inspector, set ySpeed to 3.5 while leaving xSpeed at 5.0. Walk around. In top-down 2D games, why do many classic RPGs make vertical movement slightly slower than horizontal movement?
  2. Press W and D together to move diagonally. If horizontal speed is 5 and vertical speed is 5, Pythagorean theorem says diagonal speed is (\approx 7.07\). How could you use vector normalization (vector.normalized) to keep speed constant in all directions?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare four ways to move an object in Unity (Translate, MovePosition, linearVelocity, AddForce)
  • Explain what scenarios require physics sweep functions instead of direct translation
  • Explain the relationship between code defaults and serialized Inspector overrides
  • Explain how Time.deltaTime produces identical real-world speed across differing framerates
  • Save your tuned speeds and commit your changes
